doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How work was handed out in Hollywood
summary: Carter disagrees that work isn't commensurate with talent among studio players, and mentions rejected film scores.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: To those of us not involved in Hollywood, we read and hear so much that how you get work is not always commensurate with your talents; it depends on who you know and how well you sell yourself. I think selling yourself has not been one of your primary activities. How did you actually get work during this time?
First I have to go back to a statement you just made saying that—what is it?— getting work is not always commensurate with your talent. By that what did you mean?
Well, I’m just saying what we have heard about studios in . . . well, not only studios; I guess that happens in every area that . . .

I would disagree. I would disagree with that, because I think the studio musicians in Hollywood have all been at the highest height or degree of talent or proficiency or whatever you’d call it. There were some that would certainly get more work than others, and there were certainly many who were just as good and did not get the work. You know, speaking of a clique, if you were on a certain contract as an A-list, you know, your first allegiance was to him, because you know he’s going to call you for any date that he had, and
he, if he’s a very popular and successful contractor, he would have many. But I can think of no musician that I recall who wasn’t up to the task of what he was called upon to do.
I wasn’t thinking so much of the players, the musicians, the studio musicians, so much as composers and for films.
Well, even composers in films, I’d . . .
Did the best person who would create the best possible score for a picture necessarily be the one that was chosen always?

Well, it’s not for me to say, that’s number one, and I wouldn’t know that. But I know on occasion people who have been very, very successful with musical scores for film had had their scores rejected, after even having been recorded. Some other composer would be asked to do it, to do another score. It would mean that the first composer was not capable. He just didn’t get what the director wanted. But what he had written for that particular film might have been very acceptable to someone else, and might have also been very effective to the viewer.
